abstract: Jina Hagen from Labcorp reviews cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening using massively parallel sequencing to detect fetal trisomies and subchromosomal abnormalities. She explains that fetal DNA fragments are smaller than maternal fragments, enabling fetal fraction calculation, and discusses ACOG guidelines recommending NIPT for all pregnant women. The presentation also covers the Maternity Genome reflex option for deeper sequencing when later concerns arise and emphasizes the importance of positive predictive value in counseling. Finally, she reviews carrier screening for autosomal recessive conditions, highlighting that CF and SMA screening should be offered to all patients and noting that 1-2% of couples are at risk for an affected child.
key_points: NIPT uses massively parallel sequencing to count DNA fragments from each chromosome and detect overrepresentation indicating trisomy.
Fetal DNA fragments average ~130 bp, maternal ~160 bp, allowing fetal fraction determination by size distribution.
ACOG 2020 practice bulletin 226 recommends offering NIPT to all pregnant women as the most sensitive and specific screening for trisomies.
Positive predictive value (PPV) of NIPT is ~80% overall, compared to ~3.5% for first-trimester serum screening, but PPV depends on population prevalence.
Labcorp retains the blood sample until the due date; if later ultrasound concerns arise, providers can request the Maternity Genome reflex for deeper sequencing to detect subchromosomal events.
Carrier screening for cystic fibrosis (CF) and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) should be offered to all patients regardless of ethnicity per ACOG.
Expanded carrier screening can test many conditions for the same price and is especially useful preconceptually.
Approximately 1-2% of couples are at risk for having a child with an autosomal recessive disorder.
ACOG recommends carrier screening for cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and hemoglobinopathies.
Cell-free DNA (Maternity21) can be initiated at 9 weeks and performed throughout pregnancy, with fetal fraction increasing over time.
Traditional serum screening (quad screen, first trimester screen) uses algorithms and has higher false-positive rates compared to cfDNA.
cfDNA has a screen positive rate of about 1% or less, reducing patient anxiety and unnecessary follow-up.
